This map shows the share of each country's population in extreme poverty in 2025 — earning less than $3 a day. Two hundred years ago, on the same inflation-adjusted line, roughly three-quarters of humanity would have qualified.

a thread 🧵🗺️

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

1/ The $3-a-day line is new. The World Bank raised it from $2.15 in June 2025, using updated price data. The change alone added about 125 million people to the global extreme-poverty count overnight — the ruler moved, not the reality.

2/ The long-run trend is still real. Economic historians estimate close to three-quarters of the world lived under this kind of threshold around 1820. By 2022, using the new line, the figure was about 10.5%, or 838 million people.

3/ The map's darkest countries — the Democratic Republic of Congo, Central African Republic, Madagascar — sit above 70%. That's the highest concentration of extreme poverty on Earth, packed almost entirely into one region.

4/ Notice how much of the map is blank. The US, Canada, Europe, Russia, China: none get a color here, because the World Bank doesn't track this specific measure for high-income and upper-middle-income economies — not because their rate is zero.

5/ The real story isn't decline everywhere — it's a two-century collapse in extreme poverty across almost the whole planet, with Sub-Saharan Africa left as the place progress still has to reach.

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
